CELLPHONE SNATCHERS

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Smartphones are a hot commodity - cellphone snatchers are tapping into this, targeting unsuspecting people to feed the black market

Unique Selling Point:
CCTV FOOTAGE
UNDERCOVER
BUSTS

Summary:
Times are tough. Crime is rife. And with the average smart phone costing between R15 and R30k - it’s common target for petty thieves looking to make a quick buck.

Further information:
There are three main MO’s – I think it best to include all three because it could be a thin story otherwise.
1. Smash & Grab
2. Snatching from Side Walk Restaurants
3. Runners / Walkers – while out excersing
** There’s plenty of video footage.

Some of the snatchers even work with getaway cars – if you think about the high value of the phones – it’s worth enlisting the services of your fellow criminals and turning a random petty crime into a more organised hit.

Security companies have teamed up with CCTV networks – like AI and Vumacam to track and trace some of the culprits – in many cases they use cloned number plates – but fortunately the good guys are smarter than the bad ones – and are being caught.

WHERE DO THE PHONES GO
Android phones are easier to crack and be jippo-ed to work on the networks even after they have been blacklisted. iPhones are harder to crack and are either sent out of the country or used for spare parts.

UNDERCOVER ELEMENTS
Doing a sting to try and get robbed is going to be very difficult – while there are hotspots – we could end up sitting there for days and we may not be able to catch them unless we have a camera crew and security team in place to chase them. Fortunately there is footage of these incidents.

I suggest as an alternative – we go to some of the dodgier cellphone shops and ask about sellng a phone – the only issue with this is that they may ask if it was stolen – and then technically the shop has covered itself, because it asked. So this might prove difficult. Also, we’d only be enquiring because we don’t have a smartphone that we want to sacrifice and sell for the sting.

WHY DO IT
CCTV footage. Petty crime gone organised. Security tracking and tracing criminals. Interesting insights into the black market for stolen cellphones.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Mobile devices are now a fixture of modern life. Smartphones have changed the way we interact, the way we work and the way we live.

It’s a desirable device that usually comes with a steep price tag - making it a perfect target for criminals to steal and offload quickly.

LINK: The mobile device space is suffering a smartphone crime epidemic which will only increase as the value and volume of devices continue to rise. Criminals are becoming more brazen, more cunning and more organised.
VO: CONTINUE reread for link

VO: As these devices have evolved to meet our needs, criminal tactics have also become more sophisticated.

From opportunistic thieves targeting unsuspecting people – snatching and dashing off, to violent smash and grab perpetrators – who hit motorists in traffic. But the latest modus operandi has morphed a petty crime into a more organised hit using getaway cars to flee the scene.

YLVA: People are wolves in sheep's clothing. // you suspect nothing. //NT1M16

VO: Ylva Reynolds was standing outside an antique store in Kyalami, Johannesburg when she was targeted by cellphone snatchers.

YLVA: I had my back to the driveway so I wasn't aware of the vehicle Pulling up behind us.//Next minute this guy's grabbed my phone. // INT1 M2

VO: Watch in this CCTV clip, as the guy throws her phone into the car. You see one of the shop staff struggling with the thief, as Ylva lunged after her phone.

YLVA: // I grab hold of my phone he grab. They we drive off. And then I hear these gunshots. INT 4

VO: The shop owner fired shots at the getaway car, but the thieves kept driving, dragging Ylva along.

YLVA: // my feet I'm just just being dragged and being dragged all the way all the way all the way all the way until we get to the robot. // INT5

VO: It sounds extreme for a single cellphone theft. But a top of the range smartphone is worth between 20 and 30 thousand rand - this modus operandi has become a daily reality in South Africa.

There’s been a global increase in street crime, the trafficking of stolen devices for resale, and the involvement of organized crime at all levels.

Garth de Klerk is from the Insurance Crime Bureau.

GARTH: The difference in South Africa in Africa is that the crime can be more physical // It's not just I will steal your phone if you get in my way while I do it I'll hurt you M5

VO: In Ylva’s case she eventually let go. While the thieves made off with her smartphone, she was left with a concussion, cuts and bruising.

Using cars for getaways is a trend that has become increasingly popular over the last two years explains Rob Nicol from a CCTV monitoring company.

ROB: // their main aim is to grab the cell phone jump in the vehicle and and disappear out of the area within a few minutes. M6

VO: The groups of up to three thieves make use of either a common taxi service type car or a more expensive vehicle to blend in - often the cars are cloned using fake plates - making it harder to trace - but not impossible.

With the help of neighbourhood group eBlockWatch, local security, CCTV surveillance and remote license plate recognition - the car used by Ylva’s perpetrators was picked a few weeks later - despite having fake plates.

ROB: what we were able to determine is that it was the same vehicle as it had the bullet holes in the background and the descriptions matched from the video footage we had received. INT2M4 FROM END // we immediately dispatched their CPS. The undercover unit and they were able to find the vehicle there roaming the streets// INT2M4 FROM BEGINNING

VO: While the suspects were arrested, Ylva’s phone was long gone.

LINK: This is where most stolen phones in JHB end up…. The CBD – where dodgy little cellphone shops are a dime a dozen – wheeling and dealing in stolen in cellphones – this is the first level of the mobile device black market.

VO: Rashaad Mohamed from Bad Boys Security Group showed us some of the hotspots.

CORKY: Cellphones are ending up by all the foreigners. Majority of them we talk you know Nigerians are Bangladeshis Pakistanis M6 // every street maybe every second shop probably would buy your cell phone. I mean the market is there /M8

VO: The black market for cellphones is a massive global network - explains private investigator Warren Lamont.

WARREN: what happens is is that the people who are who are in this industry in this business of getting rid of blocked phones would generally put them all in the bag consolidate them and then send them with someone who's travelling // in under a week it's been found in another country INT4M1

VO: Phones stolen in South Africa have been picked up all over the world, from countries like Nigeria and Mozambique to China, India and even the USA.

LINK: So you’ve got face recognition software, finger print access, and a passcode – you’re phone should be safe – even if it gets stolen right? Wrong. Hackers have found ways to crack these security features and even offer these services openly on the net. Once they’re into your phone – it’s free game.
VO: ACCESS - NOT EXCESS - READ IN VO
VO: Smartphones are not only stolen for resale, personal information is an even higher valued commodity - Thieves now access this confidential data stored on devices to commit other crimes.

WARREN: // one of three things is going to happen they're going to extort you for images or videos in your gallery they're going to. Secondly contact people in your contact list. Claiming that they're you asking for money //Or thirdly they're going to basically start getting into your banking and into // all sorts of passwords // And then they start to it becomes identity theft. //INT2M1

VO: Curious as to how easy it is to offload a stolen phone - we sent in an undercover agent to some of these shops.

MAC: The kind of shops that you were in to just describe them for me what did they look like. Look professional. Or is it just
AGENT: // It's not a formal shop. //. you can find the guy who put a table and there's just a small container// When you interacting with them you can see that their eyes are looking at they're not looking at me they're looking outside checking who's looking at me. //M11

VO: Even though the agent’s phone was clearly marked with the real owner’s name - there were still a number of takers.

MAC: Did any of them ask you if the phone was stolen.
AGENT: No. No one asked me therefore they were not interested in that. M7 // They were just interested in making business M5// No one even asked without about who is this v why do you have this Koekemoer phone with you. // I'm not Koekemoer, I'm black. [M7 swapped around ]

VO: The agent took in a Samsung A10 valued at R3000.

BUYER: I’ll give you R300 like this
AGENT: R300 like that?
BUYER: No
AGENT: So the software won’t be a problem?
BUYER: No i’ll open it.

VO: We paid him a visit at his little hole in the wall shop.

MAC: You’re buying stolen phones…
BUYER: no ,no no nonono I’m not buying
MAC: Are you buying cellphones ?
BUYER: No
MAC: We have you on camera - look at this - who is this?
BUYER” YEs it me
MAC It’s you - you offered him R500 for the phone - you didnt ask whether the phone is stolen…
BUYER: I didnt buy the phone...I asked him if he has proof of payment - i said i’m not gonna buy it.

VO: That’s not what happened. He loosely enquired about ownership and still made an offer.

UPSOUND SHOP 3CLip2
BUYER: where did you buy it?
AGENT: I didnt buy it
BUYER: I can give you R500

VO: No questions asked. The agent rejected the offer saying it was too low.

De Klerk says buying and selling like this - is illegal.

GARTH: // There is legislation under the second hand goods Act which would force you as a dealer to be registered in order to buy and sell electronic equipment or any second hand item// there's a series of rules // that will try and control buying and selling stolen goods M9

VO: This involves keeping a register and taking the seller’s details, copy of the ID and proof of residence, in addition to logging the phone’s serial number and noting any identifying markers.

But These shops don’t play by those rules.

CORKY: police will do an arrest, close a shop – tomorrow – someone will come and open a shop doingthe a the same thing. //M15

VO: The next shop offered us just R400 for the same phone.

UPSOUND SHOP1 CLIP 2
00.54 - AGENT - it’s new
BUYER: I understand it’s new but it’s ….pause…..secondhand… //
01.40 - AGENT: you gonna give me how much?
BUYER: Four hundred…. ja because i have to remove everything.

VO: Interested to see what they would offer for an iPhone 11 Pro valued at R27000 - we sent in a second agent.

UPSOUND FOR AGENT 2
MAC: How much did he offer you
AGENT: He offered me R1000
MAC: R1000 - did he check if it was stolen
AGENT: he say that it was stolen but he didn’t ask me anything.

VO: The buyer was keen to make deal and even started counting out cash.

We went in just minutes later to confront this eager buyer of stolen phones.

MAC - you forgot?

VO: Despite the denials - the Phones that remain in the country, are bought under the counter, and usually stripped for parts; or flashed and rebooted with a new IMEI number.

WARREN: That's basically the identification between the phone and the network. // that IMEI number // is easily changed with software on Android phone specifically. And then you can use it as a brand new handset M8 //

VO: Lamont explainsWhile iPhones are harder to crack, criminals send out phising messages to the in case of emergency contact on the stolen device - claiming the device has been found, they include a link that requires your passwords - this in turn gives the thieves access to your device and personal information.

The reality is even with built-in security features, remote tracking and data-wiping software - the best line of defence is to minimise the chance of your phone being stolen in the first place.

END SAL ALTERNATIVE SOEK
GARTH: /program yourself to what are you going to do when it happens. not if it happens these guys are desperate they are violent. liklihood doing sonemthing quite high.M20


PROMOS
PROMO 1
VO: Smartphones are high value targets for thieves. But just how far will criminals go to get your device? We investigate a new crime trend behind the black market for stolen phones.

PROMO 2
VO: Criminals go all out using getaways cars to steal pricey smartphones to make a quick buck – we go undercover to expose the growing black market for stolen phones.

PROMO 3
VO: Cellphone snatching is rife. We go undercover to investigate just how criminals offload stolen phones on the black market for a fraction of the retail value.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Smartphones are a hot commodity - cellphone snatchers are tapping into this, targeting unsuspecting people to feed the black market
metadata.Summary: Times are tough. Crime is rife. And with the average smart phone costing between R15 and R30k - it’s common target for petty thieves looking to make a quick buck.
metadata.Further information: There are three main MO’s – I think it best to include all three because it could be a thin story otherwise. 1. Smash & Grab 2. Snatching from Side Walk Restaurants 3. Runners / Walkers – while out excersing ** There’s plenty of video footage. Some of the snatchers even work with getaway cars – if you think about the high value of the phones – it’s worth enlisting the services of your fellow criminals and turning a random petty crime into a more organised hit. Security companies have teamed up with CCTV networks – like AI and Vumacam to track and trace some of the culprits – in many cases they use cloned number plates – but fortunately the good guys are smarter than the bad ones – and are being caught. WHERE DO THE PHONES GO Android phones are easier to crack and be jippo-ed to work on the networks even after they have been blacklisted. iPhones are harder to crack and are either sent out of the country or used for spare parts. UNDERCOVER ELEMENTS Doing a sting to try and get robbed is going to be very difficult – while there are hotspots – we could end up sitting there for days and we may not be able to catch them unless we have a camera crew and security team in place to chase them. Fortunately there is footage of these incidents. I suggest as an alternative – we go to some of the dodgier cellphone shops and ask about sellng a phone – the only issue with this is that they may ask if it was stolen – and then technically the shop has covered itself, because it asked. So this might prove difficult. Also, we’d only be enquiring because we don’t have a smartphone that we want to sacrifice and sell for the sting. WHY DO IT CCTV footage. Petty crime gone organised. Security tracking and tracing criminals. Interesting insights into the black market for stolen cellphones.
